cues.en: So where do you start when you have a program that's about integrating life's passions? Well, you start with why. Why? And that kicks us off for the first speaker tonight, Simon Sinek. In his talk, start with why. We assume even we know why we do what we do. But then how do you explain when things don't go as we assume? Or better,
cues.zh: 那么，当你有一个关于整合人生热情的节目时，你该从哪里开始？嗯，从“为什么”开始。为什么？这就引出了今晚的第一位讲者，Simon Sinek。在他的演讲《Start with Why》中。我们以为自己甚至知道，我们为什么做自己所做的事。但当事态不像我们设想的那样发展时，你该怎么解释？或者更好地说，

cues.en: How do you explain when others are able to achieve things that seem to defy all of the assumptions? For example, why is Apple so innovative? Year after year after year after year, they're more innovative than all their competition. And yet, they're just a computer company. They're just like everyone else. They have the same access to the same talent, the same agencies, the same consultants, the same media. Then why is it that they seem to have something different? Why is it that Martin Luther King
cues.zh: 你该怎么解释，别人能够取得似乎推翻所有假设的成就？比如，为什么 Apple 如此创新？一年又一年，一年又一年，他们比所有竞争对手都更有创新力。可他们只是一家电脑公司。他们和其他人一样。他们同样能接触到同样的人才、同样的代理机构、同样的顾问、同样的媒体。那为什么他们似乎拥有某种不同的东西？为什么 Martin Luther King

cues.en: led the civil rights movement. He wasn't the only man who suffered in a pre-civil rights America, and he certainly wasn't the only great orator of the day. Why him? And why is it that the Wright brothers were able to figure out controlled powered man flight when there were certainly other teams who were better qualified, better funded, and they didn't achieve powered man flight, and the Wright brothers beat them to it. There's something else at play here. About three and a half years ago,
cues.zh: 领导了民权运动。他并不是民权运动前的美国唯一受苦的人，也当然不是当时唯一伟大的演说家。为什么是他？还有，为什么 Wright 兄弟能够弄明白可控载人动力飞行，而当时肯定有其他团队更有资格、资金更充足，却没有实现载人动力飞行，反而让 Wright 兄弟抢先一步？这里还有别的因素在起作用。大约三年半前，

cues.en: I made a discovery, and this discovery profoundly changed my view on how I thought the world worked, and it even profoundly changed the way in which I operate in it. As it turns out, there's a pattern. As it turns out, all the great and inspiring leaders and organizations in the world, whether it's Apple or Martin Luther King or the Wright Brothers, they all think, act, and communicate the exact same way, and it's the complete opposite to everyone else.
cues.zh: 我发现了一件事，而这个发现深刻改变了我对世界如何运作的看法，甚至深刻改变了我在其中行事的方式。事实证明，存在一种模式。事实证明，世界上所有伟大而鼓舞人心的领导者和组织，无论是 Apple、Martin Luther King 还是 Wright 兄弟，他们的思考、行动和沟通方式都完全相同，而且和其他所有人完全相反。

cues.en: All I did was codify it. And it's probably the world's simplest idea. I call it the Golden Circle. Why, how, what? This little idea explains why some organizations and some leaders are able to inspire where others aren't. Let me define the terms really quickly. Every single person, every single organization on the planet knows what they do, 100%. Some...
cues.zh: 我所做的只是把它归纳成法则。这大概是世界上最简单的理念。我称之为黄金圈。为什么、怎么做、是什么？这个小理念解释了为什么有些组织和领导者能够激励他人，而另一些不能。让我很快定义一下这些术语。地球上的每一个人、每一个组织都百分之百知道自己做什么。有些人……

cues.en: know how they do it, whether you call it your differentiating value proposition or your proprietary process or your USP. But very, very few people or organizations know why they do what they do. And by why, I don't mean to make a profit. That's a result. It's always a result. By why, I mean, what's your purpose? What's your cause? What's your belief? Why does your organization exist? Well, as a result, the way we think, the way we act, the way we communicate is from the outside in. It's obvious. We go from the clearest thing
cues.zh: 知道自己怎么做，不管你把这叫做差异化价值主张、专有流程，还是你的 USP。但非常非常少的人或组织知道自己为什么做自己所做的事。而所谓“为什么”，我不是指赚钱。那是结果。它始终是结果。所谓“为什么”，我指的是：你的目的是什么？你的事业是什么？你的信念是什么？你的组织为什么存在？于是，结果就是，我们思考的方式、行动的方式、沟通的方式都是由外而内。这很明显。我们从最清楚的东西

cues.en: to the fuzziest thing. But the inspired leaders and the inspired organizations, regardless of their size, regardless of their industry, all think, act, and communicate from the inside out. Let me give you an example. I use Apple because they're easy to understand and everybody gets it. If Apple were like everyone else, a marketing message from them might sound like this. We make great computers. They're beautifully designed, simple to use, and user friendly.
cues.zh: 到最模糊的东西。但受启发的领导者和受启发的组织，无论规模大小，无论行业，都从内而外思考、行动和沟通。让我举个例子。我用 Apple，因为他们容易理解，大家都懂。如果 Apple 和其他人一样，他们的营销信息可能会是这样：我们制造很棒的电脑。它们设计精美、使用简单、对用户友好。

cues.en: Want to buy one? Meh. And that's how most of us communicate. That's how most marketing is done. That's how most sales is done. And that's how most of us communicate interpersonally. We say what we do. We say how we're different or how we better. And we expect some sort of behavior, a purchase, a vote, something like that. Here's our new law firm. We have the best lawyers with the biggest clients. We always perform for our clients to do business with us. Here's our new car. It gets great gas mileage. It has leather seats by our car. But it's uninspiring. Here's how Apple
cues.zh: 想买一个吗？呃，没什么感觉。我们大多数人就是这么沟通的。大多数营销就是这么做的。大多数销售也是这么做的。我们大多数人私下交流时也是这样。我们说自己是做什么的。我们说我们有何不同，或者我们哪里更胜一筹。然后期待对方做出某种行为：购买、投票之类的。这是我们的新律所。我们拥有最好的律师，服务最大的客户。我们总是为客户全力以赴，以促成合作。这是我们的新车。它非常省油。它配有真皮座椅，买我们的车吧。但它毫无吸引力。Apple 是这样做的：

cues.en: actually communicates. Everything we do, we believe in challenging the status quo. We believe in thinking differently. The way we challenge the status quo is by making our products beautifully designed, simple to use, and user friendly. We just happen to make great computers. Want to buy one? Totally different, right? Be ready to buy a computer from me.
cues.zh: 真正传达出来。我们所做的一切，都相信要挑战现状。我们相信要与众不同地思考。我们挑战现状的方式，就是把产品设计得精美、简单易用、对人友好。我们只是恰好做出了很棒的电脑。想买一台吗？完全不一样，对吧？准备好从我这儿买台电脑吧。

cues.en: All I did was reverse the order of the information. People don't buy what you do, people buy why you do it. People don't buy what you do, they buy why you do it. This explains why every single person in this room is perfectly comfortable buying a computer from Apple. But we're also perfectly comfortable buying an MP3 player from Apple, or a phone from Apple, or a DVR from Apple.
cues.zh: 我所做的只是把信息的顺序颠倒过来。人们买的不是你做的事，而是你做这件事的原因。人们买的不是你做的事，而是你为什么做。这就解释了为什么在座的每一个人都能毫无顾虑地买苹果的电脑。但我们也同样能毫无顾虑地买苹果的 MP3 播放器、苹果的手机，或者苹果的 DVR。

cues.en: But as I said before, Apple's just a computer company. There's nothing that distinguishes them structurally from any of their competitors. Their competitors are all equally qualified to make all of these products. In fact, they tried. A few years ago, Gateway came out with flat screen TVs. They're eminently qualified to make flat screen TVs. They've been making flat screen monitors for years. Nobody bought one. Dell came out with MP3 players and PDAs. And they make great quality products, and they can make perfectly well-designed products. And nobody bought one.
cues.zh: 正如我之前说的，苹果只是一家电脑公司。从结构上讲，他们和任何竞争对手都没有区别。他们的竞争对手同样完全有能力做出所有这些产品。事实上，他们也试过。几年前，Gateway 推出了平板电视。他们完全有资格做平板电视。他们做平板显示器已经很多年了。可没人买。Dell 推出了 MP3 播放器和 PDA。他们能做出质量很好的产品，也完全能做出设计精良的产品。可还是没人买。

cues.en: In fact, talking about it now, we can't even imagine buying an MP3 player from Dell. Why would you buy an MP3 player from a computer company? But we do it every day. People don't buy what you do, they buy why you do it. The goal is not to do business with everybody who needs what you have. The goal is to do business with people who believe what you believe. Here's the best part. None of what I'm telling you is my opinion. It's all grounded in the tenets of biology, not psychology.
cues.zh: 事实上，现在说起来，我们甚至无法想象从 Dell 买 MP3 播放器。你为什么会从一家电脑公司买 MP3 播放器？但我们每天都在这么做。人们买的不是你做什么，而是你为什么做。目标不是和所有需要你所提供之物的人做生意。目标是和相信你所相信的人做生意。最棒的是，我告诉你的这些都不是我的观点。它全都建立在生物学而非心理学的原理之上。

cues.en: biology. If you look at a cross-section of the human brain looking from the top down, what you see is the human brain is actually broken into three major components that correlate perfectly with the golden circle. Our newest brain, our homo sapien brain, our neocortex, corresponds with the what level. The neocortex is responsible for all of our rational and analytical thought and language. The middle two sections make up our limbic brains, and our limbic brains are responsible for all of our feelings.
cues.zh: 生物学原理。如果你从上往下看人脑的截面，就会发现人脑其实分为三大主要部分，它们与黄金圈法则完美契合。我们最新进化出的大脑，也就是智人大脑、大脑新皮层，对应的是“做什么”层面。新皮层负责我们所有的理性与分析性思维，以及语言能力。中间的两部分构成了边缘脑，而边缘脑则负责我们所有的情感与感受。

cues.en: like trust and loyalty. It's also responsible for all human behavior, all decision-making, and it has no capacity for language. In other words, when we communicate from the outside in, yes, people can understand vast amounts of complicated information like features and benefits and facts and figures. It just doesn't drive behavior. When we communicate from the inside out, we're talking directly to the part of the brain.
cues.zh: 比如信任和忠诚。它还负责所有人类行为、所有决策，却没有语言能力。换句话说，当我们由外而内地沟通时，没错，人们能理解大量复杂信息，比如功能、好处、事实和数据。但这并不会驱动行为。当我们由内而外地沟通时，我们是在直接对大脑中

cues.en: that controls behavior, and then we allow people to rationalize it with the tangible things we say and do. This is where gut decisions come from. You know, sometimes you can give somebody all the facts and your figures, and they say, I know what all the facts and details say, but it just doesn't feel right. Why would we use that verb? It doesn't feel right, because the part of the brain that controls decision-making doesn't control language. And the best we can muster up is, I don't know, it just doesn't feel right.
cues.zh: 控制行为的那部分说话，然后让人们用我们所说所做的具体事物为它找理由。直觉决策就来自这里。你知道，有时你给某人所有的事实和数据，他们会说：我知道所有事实和细节说明了什么，但就是感觉不对。为什么我们会用这个动词？感觉不对，是因为控制决策的那部分大脑不控制语言。而我们最多只能说出：我不知道，就是感觉不对。

cues.en: Or sometimes you say you're leading with your heart or you're leading with your soul. Well, I hate to break it to you. Those aren't other body parts controlling your behavior. It's all happening here in your limbic brain, the part of the brain that controls decision-making and not language. But if you don't know why you do what you do, and people respond to why you do what you do, then how will you ever get people to vote for you or buy something from you, or more importantly, be loyal and want to be a part of what it is that you do?
cues.zh: 或者有时你说你是在跟着心走，或跟着灵魂走。好吧，我不想打击你。那些并不是控制你行为的其他身体部位。这一切都发生在你的边缘脑，也就是大脑中控制决策、不控制语言的那部分。但如果你不知道自己为什么做你所做的事，而人们又回应你做事的“为什么”，那你怎么能让人们投票给你、买你的东西，更重要的是，对你忠诚并想成为你所做之事的一部分？

cues.en: Again, the goal is not just to sell people who need what you have. The goal is to sell the people who believe what you believe. The goal is not just to hire people who need a job. It's to hire people who believe what you believe. I always say that if you hire people just because they can do a job, they'll work for your money. But if you hire people who believe what you believe, they work for you with blood and sweat and tears. And nowhere else is there a better example of this than with the Wright Brothers.
cues.zh: 再说一次，目标不只是把东西卖给需要它的人。目标是卖给相信你所相信的人。目标不只是招聘需要一份工作的人。而是招聘相信你所相信的人。我一直说，如果你只是因为一个人能干活就雇用他，他会为你的钱工作。但如果你雇用相信你所相信的人，他们会为你流血流汗流泪地工作。没有比 Wright Brothers 更好的例子了。

cues.en: Most people don't know about Samuel Pierpont Langley. And back in the early 20th century, the pursuit of powered man flight was like the dot-com of the day. Everybody was trying it. And Samuel Pierpont Langley had what we assumed to be the recipe for success. I mean, even now, when you ask people, why did your product or why did your company fail? And people always give you the same permutation of the same three things. Under-capitalized, the wrong people, bad market conditions. It's always the same three things.
cues.zh: 大多数人都不知道 Samuel Pierpont Langley。回到20世纪初，追求载人动力飞行就像当时的互联网热潮。人人都在尝试。而 Samuel Pierpont Langley 拥有我们以为的成功配方。我是说，即使现在，当你问人们，你的产品为什么失败，或者你的公司为什么失败？人们总会给你同样三件事的不同排列组合。资金不足、用错人、市场环境不佳。总是同样的三件事。

cues.en: So let's explore that. Samuel Pierpont Langley was given $50,000 by the War Department to figure out this flying machine. Money was no problem. He held a seat at Harvard and worked at the Smithsonian and was extremely well connected. He knew all the big minds of the day. He hired the best minds money could find, and the market conditions were fantastic. The New York Times followed him around everywhere, and everyone was rooting for Langley. And how come we've never heard?
cues.zh: 我们来探讨一下这一点。Samuel Pierpont Langley 曾从美国战争部获得五万美元来研发飞行器。资金完全不是问题。他在 Harvard 拥有席位，在 Smithsonian 任职，而且人脉极广。他结识当时所有的顶级泰斗。他不惜重金聘请最优秀的头脑，市场条件也极其有利。The New York Times 对他全程跟拍，所有人都看好 Langley。但为什么我们却从未听说过？

cues.en: of Samuel Pierpont Langley. A few hundred miles away in Dayton, Ohio, Orville and Wilbur Wright. They had none of what we consider to be the recipe for success. They had no money. They paid for their dream with the proceeds from their bicycle shop. Not a single person on the Wright Brothers team had a college education, not even Orville or Wilbur. And the New York Times followed them around nowhere. The difference was Orville and Wilbur
cues.zh: Samuel Pierpont Langley 这个人？而在几百英里外的俄亥俄州 Dayton，Orville 和 Wilbur Wright 兄弟。他们完全不具备我们所认为的任何成功要素。他们没有钱。他们是用自己自行车店的微薄收入来支撑梦想。Wright Brothers 团队中没有一个人接受过大学教育，连 Orville 和 Wilbur 自己也没有。也没有 The New York Times 跟随报道他们。不同之处在于，Orville 和 Wilbur

cues.en: were driven by a cause, by a purpose, by a belief. They believed that if they could figure out this flying machine, it'll change the course of the world. Samuel Pierpont Langley was different. He wanted to be rich and he wanted to be famous. He was in pursuit of the result. He was in pursuit of the riches. And lo and behold, look what happened. The people who believed in the Wright Brothers' dream worked with them with blood and sweat and tears. The others just worked for the paycheck.
cues.zh: 是被一种事业、目标和信念所驱动的。他们坚信，只要能造出这架飞行器，就能改变世界的进程。Samuel Pierpont Langley 则不同。他想要发财，想要出名。他追求的是结果。他追求的是财富。结果你们看，后来发生了什么。那些认同 Wright Brothers 梦想的人，和他们一起流血流汗、倾注心血。而另外那帮人仅仅是在为了薪水打工。

cues.en: And they tell stories of how every time the Wright Brothers went out, they would have to take five sets of parts, because that's how many times they would crash before they came in for supper. And eventually, on December 17, 1903, the Wright Brothers took flight. And no one was there to even experience it. We found out about it a few days later. And further proof that Langley was motivated by the wrong thing, the day the Wright Brothers took flight, he quit.
cues.zh: 相传 Wright Brothers 每次出门试飞，都得带上五套备用零件，因为在回家吃晚饭前他们往往会坠毁那么多次。最终，在 1903 年 12 月 17 日，Wright Brothers 成功起飞了。当时甚至没有人在场见证这一刻。人们在几天后才得知这个消息。而更进一步证明 Langley 动机不纯的是：就在 Wright Brothers 成功试飞的那一天，他放弃了。

cues.en: He could have said, that's an amazing discovery, guys, and I will improve upon your technology. But he didn't. He wasn't first. He didn't get rich. He didn't get famous. So he quit. People don't buy what you do, they buy why you do it. And if you talk about what you believe, you will attract those who believe what you believe. Well, why is it important to attract those who believe what you believe? Something called the law of diffusion of innovation. And if you don't know the law, you definitely know the terminology. The first 2.5% of our population
cues.zh: 他本可以说：“伙计们，这是个了不起的发现，我会在你们的技术基础上继续改进。”但他没有。他没能拿到第一。他没能发家致富。他没能名声大噪。所以他退出了。人们买的不是你“做什么”，而是你“为什么做”。如果你谈论自己的信念，就会吸引那些认同你信念的人。那么，为什么吸引认同你信念的人如此重要？这源于所谓的“创新扩散定律”。就算你不知道这个定律，也一定听说过它的术语。人群中最初的 2.5%

cues.en: are our innovators. The next 13.5% of our population are our early adopters. The next 34% are your early majority, your late majority, and your laggards. The only reason these people buy touch-tone phones is because you can't buy rotary phones anymore. We all sit at various places at various times on this scale, but what the law of diffusion of innovation tells us is that if you want mass market success or mass market acceptance of an idea, you cannot have it until you achieve
cues.zh: 是创新者。接下来的 13.5% 是早期采用者。接下来的 34% 是早期大众，随后是晚期大众，最后是落后者。这些落后者之所以会买按键电话，唯一的原因是市场上已经买不到旋转拨号电话了。在不同时期，我们每个人都会处于这条曲线的不同位置，但创新扩散定律告诉我们，如果你想获得大众市场的成功，或者让某个理念被大众市场所接受，就必须先达到

cues.en: this tipping point between 15% and 18% market penetration, and then the system tips. And I love asking businesses, what's your conversion on new business? And they love to tell you, oh, it's about 10% proudly. Well, you can trip over 10% of the customers. We all have about 10% who just get it. That's how we describe them. That's like that gut feeling. Oh, they just get it. The problem is, how do you find the ones that just get it before you're doing business with them versus the ones who don't get it? So it's this here, this little gap.
cues.zh: 15% 到 18% 市场渗透率这个引爆点，然后整个体系才会迎来质变。我特别喜欢问一些企业：“你们新业务的转化率是多少？”他们总是自豪地回答：“哦，大概 10% 左右。”其实，随便撞大运你都能碰上 10% 的客户。我们总能遇到大约 10%“一听就懂”的人。我们就是这么形容他们的。就像那种直觉：“噢，他们一听就懂。”问题在于，在正式合作之前，你如何找出那些“一听就懂”的人，并区分出那些“完全不感冒”的人？问题就在这里，就在这小小的差距。

cues.en: that you have to close, as Jeffrey Moore calls it, crossing the chasm. Because you see, the early majority will not try something until someone else has tried it first. And these guys, the innovators and the early adopters, they're comfortable making those gut decisions. They're more comfortable making those intuitive decisions that are driven by what they believe about the world, and not just what product is available.
cues.zh: 你必须跨越的，正如 Jeffrey Moore 所说，跨越鸿沟。因为你看，早期大众要等别人先试过，才会去尝试。而这些人，创新者和早期采用者，很习惯凭直觉拍板。他们更习惯做那种由世界观驱动的直觉决定，而不只是看市面上有什么产品。

cues.en: These are the people who stood online for six hours to buy an iPhone when they first came out, when you could have just walked into the store the next week and bought one off the shelf. These are the people who spent $40,000 on flat-screen TVs when they first came out, even though the technology was substandard. And by the way, they didn't do it, because the technology was so great. They did it for themselves. It's because they wanted to be first. People don't buy what you do, they buy why you do it, and what you do simply proves what you believe.
cues.zh: 这些人，就是 iPhone 刚出时排六小时队去买的人，其实下周走进店里就能从货架上买到。这些人，就是平板电视刚出时花 4 万美元去买的人，尽管当时技术还不达标。顺便说，他们不是因为这技术多棒才买，他们是为自己而买。因为他们想成为第一批。人们买的不是你做的是什么，而是你为什么做；你做的东西只是证明你的信念。

cues.en: In fact, people will do the things that prove what they believe. The reason that person bought the iPhone in the first six hours or stood in line for six hours was because of what they believed about the world and how they wanted everybody to see them. They were first. People don't buy what you do, they buy why you do it. So let me give you a famous example, a famous failure and a famous success of the law of diffusion of innovation. First, the famous failure. It's a commercial example.
cues.zh: 事实上，人们会做那些能证明自己信念的事。那个人在前六小时买下 iPhone，或者排队六小时，是因为他们对世界的信念，以及他们希望别人怎么看他们。他们是第一批。人们买的不是你做的是什么，而是你为什么做。让我给你们一个著名例子，创新扩散定律的一个著名失败和一个著名成功。先说那个著名失败。这是个商业案例。

cues.en: We said before, a second ago, the recipe for success is money and the right people and the right marketing conditions, right? You should have success then. Look at TiVo. From the time TiVo came out, about eight or nine years ago, to this current day, they are the single highest quality product on the market. Hands down, there is no dispute. They were extremely well-funded. Market conditions were fantastic. I mean, we use TiVo as a verb. I like TiVo stuff on my piece of junk Time Warner DVR all the time. But TiVo is a commercial failure.
cues.zh: 我们刚才说过，成功的配方是资金、合适的人、合适的市场条件，对吧？那你就该成功。看看 TiVo。从大约八九年前 TiVo 推出到现在，它一直是市场上质量最高的产品。毫无疑问，没有争议。他们资金极其充足。市场条件非常好。我是说，我们把 TiVo 当动词用。我一直喜欢把节目 TiVo 到我那台破旧的 Time Warner DVR 上。但 TiVo 是个商业失败。

cues.en: they've never made money. And when they went IPO, their stock was at about $30 or $40, and then plummeted, and it's never traded above $10. In fact, I don't think so. It's even traded above $6, except for a couple of little spikes. Because you see, when TiVo launched their product, they told us all what they had. They said, we have a product that pauses live TV, skips commercials, rewinds live TV, and memorizes your viewing habits without you even asking.
cues.zh: 他们从没赚过钱。IPO 时股价大约 30 或 40 美元，然后暴跌，之后再也没有超过 10 美元交易。事实上，我觉得连 6 美元都很少超过，只有几次小幅反弹。因为你看，TiVo 推出产品时，告诉我们的是他们有什么。他们说，我们有一款产品，能暂停直播电视、跳过广告、倒回直播电视，还能在你没要求的情况下记住你的收视习惯。

cues.en: And the cynical majority said, we don't believe you. We don't need it. We don't like it. You're scaring us. What if they had said, if you're the kind of person who likes to have total control over every aspect of your life, boy, do we have a product for you. It pauses live TV, skips commercials, memorizes your viewing habits, et cetera, et cetera. People don't buy what you do, they buy why you do it, and what you do simply serves as the proof.
cues.zh: 而怀疑的大多数说，我们不信你。我们不需要。我们不喜欢。你在吓我们。要是他们说，如果你是那种喜欢完全掌控生活方方面面的人，天哪，我们正好有一款产品给你。它能暂停直播电视、跳过广告、记住你的收视习惯，等等等等。人们买的不是你做的是什么，而是你为什么做；你做的东西只是作为证明。

cues.en: of what you believe. Now let me give you a successful example of the law of diffusion of innovation. In the summer of 1963, 250,000 people showed up on the mall in Washington to hear Dr. King speak. They sent out no invitations and there was no website to check the date. How do you do that? Well...
cues.zh: 你所相信的东西。现在让我给你一个创新扩散定律的成功例子。1963年夏天，25万人聚集在华盛顿国家广场，听金博士演讲。他们没有发出任何邀请，也没有网站可以查询日期。他们是怎么做到的？嗯……

cues.en: Dr. King wasn't the only man in America who was a great orator. He wasn't the only man in America who suffered in a pre-civil rights America. In fact, some of his ideas were bad, but he had a gift. He didn't go around telling people what needed to change in America. He went around and told people what he believed. I believe, I believe, I believe, he told people. And people who believed what he believed took his cause, and they made it their own, and they told people. And some of those people...
cues.zh: 金博士并不是美国唯一伟大的演说家。他也不是美国唯一在民权运动前的美国遭受苦难的人。事实上，他有些想法并不好，但他有一种天赋。他没有四处告诉人们美国需要改变什么。他四处告诉人们他相信什么。我相信，我相信，我相信，他这样告诉人们。而那些相信他所相信的人接过他的事业，把它变成自己的事业，并告诉其他人。其中一些人……

cues.en: created structures to get the word out to even more people. And lo and behold, 250,000 people showed up on the right day, on the right time, to hear him speak. How many of them showed up for him? Zero. They showed up for themselves. It's what they believed about America that got them to travel on a bus for eight hours to stand in the sun in Washington in the middle of August.
cues.zh: 建立起组织，把消息传给更多人。瞧，25万人在正确的那一天、正确的时间出现，来听他演讲。他们中有多少人是为他而来？零。他们是为自己而来。正是他们对美国的信念，让他们坐八小时巴士，在八月中旬的华盛顿站在太阳下。

cues.en: It's what they believed, and it wasn't about black versus white. 25% of the audience was white. Dr. King believed that there were two types of laws in this world, those that are made by a higher authority and those that are made by man. And not until all the laws that are made by man are consistent with the laws that are made by the higher authority will we live in a just world. It just so happens that the Civil Rights Movement was the perfect thing to help him bring his cause to life.
cues.zh: 这是他们所相信的，而且无关黑人与白人的对立。听众中25%是白人。金博士相信世界上有两种法律：由更高权威制定的法律，和由人制定的法律。只有当所有由人制定的法律都与由更高权威制定的法律一致时，我们才能生活在一个公正的世界里。恰好，民权运动正是帮助他把自己的事业变为现实的完美载体。

cues.en: We followed him, not for him, but for ourselves. And by the way, he gave the I Have a Dream speech, not the I Have a Plan speech. Listen to politicians now with their comprehensive 12-point plans. They're not inspiring anybody. Because there are leaders and there are those who lead. Leaders hold a position of power or authority, but those who lead inspire us. Whether they're individuals or organizations, we follow those who lead, not because we have to, but because we want to.
cues.zh: 我们追随他，不是为他，而是为我们自己。顺便说一句，他发表的是《I Have a Dream》演讲，不是《I Have a Plan》演讲。听听现在的政客，带着他们全面的12点计划。他们激励不了任何人。因为有些人是领导者，有些人是引领者。领导者拥有权力或权威职位，但引领者激励我们。无论他们是个人还是组织，我们追随那些引领者，不是因为我们不得不，而是因为我们想要。

cues.en: We follow those who lead, not for them, but for ourselves. And it's those who start with why that have the ability to inspire those around them or find others who inspire them. Thank you very much.
cues.zh: 我们追随那些引领者，不是为他们，而是为我们自己。正是那些从为什么开始的人，有能力激励身边的人，或找到能激励他们的人。非常感谢。
